questions.question: What does the Gen Z blame the previous generations (Boomers, GenX, / Millennials) for?

  • prompting previous generations to rethink how we approach life, work, and leisure, and to
  • locate the true value at the centre of many processes. Millennials experienced several
  • economic crises like the Great Recession of 2008. In 2019, it was calculated that Millennials
  • earn 20% less than the Boomers did at the same age, and live with daily anxiety levels about
  • the loss of a job. Gen Z-no concern for careers- as no guarantee of a stable career future.
  • They use digital tools, platforms and services in order to restore life control that they perceive
  • the Millennials lost. K

questions.question: In what way does Brock portray technology as an invasion of privacy within his home in the story "The Murderer"? Discuss why the narrator in "Password" initially resists the idea of having a new
questions.solution_html:
• In "The Murderer" by Ray Bradbury, Brock portrays technology as an invasion of privacy
  • showing how electronic devices constantly intrude into every aspect of his personal life.

  • electronic systems interrupting his peace at all hours. Brock feels that machines have taken
  • control of his life, deciding what he hears, sees, and experiences, leaving him with little
  • personal freedom. His violent rejection of the machines symbolizes his desire to reclaim
  • privacy and human freedom. An

questions.question: How do ordinary people manage their data? What can be done to regulate ownership of data?
questions.solution_html:

  • individually they have little real power against large corporations such as Google and
  • Facebook that harvest data. Nationalisation of data by governments could offer one solution

questions.question: / Vashti’s journey, Kuno’s room, and his confession highlight the dependence on the Machine? How does Ray Bradbury use exaggeration to critique society’s obsession with
questions.solution_html:
• Vashti, in E.M. Forster’s “The Machine Stops”, lives in total dependence on the Machine
  • — no human contact, air, light, and even ideas — her son Kuno insists that she visit him in
  • person, rejecting the Machine's mediated version of connection. Her journey exposes how
  • deeply "advanced" humanity has come to fear direct experience, as she reacts with horror to
  • sunlight, smell, and human touch. Unlike other rooms, Kuno's room symbolises resistance.
  • He questions the Machine's authority and longs for freedom. His room becomes a place
  • where independent thought survives, contrasting with the Machine's blind worship and
  • foreshadowing its destructive power. Kuno confesses to Vashti that he escaped to the Earth's
  • surface and discovered that the outside world is still habitable. In the end, Vashti and Kuno
  • are reunited as the Machine collapses, recognising that humanity's blind faith in technology
  • has led to its downfall. An
questions.final_answer: has led to its downfall. An
questions.source_exam: III Semester MGU-UGP-(Hons) 2024 Admission Regular(Special Examination) Examination July 2026

questions.question: / communication devices in "The Murderer"?
questions.solution_html:
• Ray Bradbury exaggerates the sheer saturation of communication technology in “The
  • Murderer” — offices piped with clashing soundtracks, a house that talks in every room, and a
  • bus full of commuters narrating their location to spouses — satirising how "convenience" has
  • metastasised into constant noise. Brock's reactions are levelled up to comic gestures (bite a
  • wrist radio in half, shoot a television six times, and spoon ice cream into a car radio
  • transmitter, turning ordinary appliance)-hatred into absurd, dramatic "murders" that expose
  • the disproportionate grip these devices hold over daily life. Through ‘anthropomorphism’- the
  • front door that "shrills," the stove that "screams," — Bradbury depicts machines as living
  • tyrants, making Brock's violence feel like self-defence rather than vandalism, which sharpens
  • the critique of how technology has usurped human agency. The image of the psychiatrist
  • absorbed into a barrage of ringing phones— after diagnosing Brock as "disoriented" —
  • delivers Bradbury's sharpest exaggeration and irony: society is so completely saturated by
  • devices that even the man meant to cure obsession is himself trapped by it, showing the
  • addiction to be systemic rather than individual. An
questions.final_answer: addiction to be systemic rather than individual. An
questions.source_exam: III Semester MGU-UGP-(Hons) 2024 Admission Regular(Special Examination) Examination July 2026

  • Linnea's invitation to a stranger to paint,shows the shifting authority to individual- Kritzer

questions.solution_html:
• Vashti, in E.M. Forster’s “The Machine Stops”, lives in total dependence on the Machine

  • surface and discovered that the outside world is still habitable. In the end, Vashti and Kuno
  • are reunited as the Machine collapses, recognising that humanity's blind faith in technology

questions.question: / communication devices in "The Murderer"?
questions.solution_html:
• Ray Bradbury exaggerates the sheer saturation of communication technology in “The
  • Murderer” — offices piped with clashing soundtracks, a house that talks in every room, and a
  • bus full of commuters narrating their location to spouses — satirising how "convenience" has
  • metastasised into constant noise. Brock's reactions are levelled up to comic gestures (bite a
  • wrist radio in half, shoot a television six times, and spoon ice cream into a car radio
  • transmitter, turning ordinary appliance)-hatred into absurd, dramatic "murders" that expose
  • the disproportionate grip these devices hold over daily life. Through ‘anthropomorphism’- the
  • front door that "shrills," the stove that "screams," — Bradbury depicts machines as living
  • tyrants, making Brock's violence feel like self-defence rather than vandalism, which sharpens
  • the critique of how technology has usurped human agency. The image of the psychiatrist
  • absorbed into a barrage of ringing phones— after diagnosing Brock as "disoriented" —
  • delivers Bradbury's sharpest exaggeration and irony: society is so completely saturated by
  • devices that even the man meant to cure obsession is himself trapped by it, showing the
  • addiction to be systemic rather than individual. An
questions.final_answer: addiction to be systemic rather than individual. An
